newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Shi'ite leader's death sparks clashes in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Shi'ite leader's death sparks clashes in Pakistan.

text.p: Gunmen killed a local Shi'ite Moslem leader on Friday in the Pakistani town of Derya Khan, in Punjab province, triggering clashes between supporters of militant Sunni and Shi'ite groups, police and witnesses said.
Police said two men on a motorcycle shot dead Sayed Ijaz Hussain, the president of the local branch of the Shi'ite Tehrik-i-Jafria Pakistan (TJP) organisation.
Hussain was hit by a burst of fire from a Kalashnikov assault rifle as he was sitting outside with at least 10 people, one of whom was shot in both legs when he pursued the attackers.
No group claimed responsibility for the attack, which appeared to be the latest episode in a long-running feud between hardline Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem factions in Punjab.

Witnesses said angry TJP supporters took to the streets in protest after Hussain's killing, only to be challenged by rival Sunni demonstrators. Gunfire echoed through the town and officials said a Sunni man had suffered a leg wound.
Police reinforcements from surrounding districts arrived on the scene to pacify the rival groups.
Witnesses said at least two shops had been attacked and their goods had been burned in the street. Demonstrators set tyres ablaze and fired into the air.

"Now by the grace of God things are under control," one local official said by telephone. "The funeral (of Hussain) is due to take place at 8:00 p.m. (1500 GMT), so it's a sensitive time, but we have prepared for all these things."
More than 110 people have been killed in Sunni-Shi'ite violence, most of them in targeted attacks, in Pakistan this year. Communal clashes have been extremely rare.
Police have rounded up scores of religious activists in Punjab this week in an effort to contain the vendetta.
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif told provincial chief ministers at a meeting in Islamabad on Thursday to take immediate steps to curb lawlessness and sectarian violence, newspapers reported.
